claims.text: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni baseline is single-phase FCC after standardized thermomechanical processing.
Co is a costly constituent whose concentration should be reduced for cost optimization.
Reducing Co or other costly constituents systematically decreases atomic size misfit in Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni subsets.
The largest calculated atomic misfit in equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni is about 4.1% between Cr and Co or Fe.
Reducing costly constituents alters the development and nature of short-range atomic order.
Atomic size mismatch contributes to solid-solution strengthening in equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni.
Lower atomic size misfit reduces lattice distortion.
Changes in short-range order alter dislocation mobility.
Reduced lattice distortion and modified short-range order create fewer or less severe obstacles to dislocation motion.
Changing principal-element concentrations can change solid-solution strengthening while retaining a single-phase solid solution.
Identical thermomechanical schedules and test conditions isolate intrinsic compositional effects on mechanical behavior.
Cost-optimized alloys with reduced costly constituents will have modestly lower yield strength than equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni.
Cost-optimized alloys will have improved ductility relative to equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni.
Cost-optimized alloys may have enhanced strain-rate sensitivity relative to equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni.
Lattice-distortion and short-range-order metrics should correlate systematically with yield strength, ductility, or strain-rate sensitivity.
The proposed relationship is limited to single-phase FCC alloys and may fail when phase separation, precipitation, or gross microstructural inhomogeneity occurs.
Minor clustering or grain-boundary chemistry changes may also influence the measured mechanical properties.
